I am 70 years old now, and I have been farming this land in Quzhou County for half a century. My legs ache when the weather changes, but my hands still remember what to do. I only went to primary school, but the land has been my true teacher. This year, my 18 mu will be split between the winter wheat already in the ground since last autumn, the cotton I will plant this spring, and the summer maize that follows the wheat harvest.

I keep 10 mu for wheat and maize together — that gives us grain to eat and some to sell. The wheat needs three irrigations from my well: at green-up, at jointing, and when the grains are filling. I buy improved wheat seed from the county supply station because it is reliable, and I spread about 15 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphate, and 4 kg of potash per mu. I do not chase record yields anymore — steady and sure is better at my age.

For cotton, I will plant 8 mu this year. Cotton is backbreaking work — planting, pruning, spraying, picking — and with my children working in the county town factories, I cannot manage any more than that. Cotton needs deep ploughing, at least 20 cm, so the roots can dig down deep. I will irrigate three times, especially at flowering and boll-setting, and I must spray five times for bollworms. If I skip even one spraying, the worms will ruin everything.

After the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant hybrid maize that very day — you cannot waste a single day of the summer season. Hybrid maize grows fast, and with two irrigations and some fertilizer, it will give a decent crop by September. I use rotary tillage for wheat and maize to save my old back and save time, but cotton still needs the plough. My well gives me water, but pumping costs electricity, so I only water when the crops truly need it. After 50 years, I can tell by looking at the leaves.
